power.title: Letters from Lanuvium
power.flavour: Your letters reach Brutus at his villa, sealed, copied and passed hand to hand.

law.title: The Dictatorship Abolished Forever
law.flavour: No man shall propose the dictatorship, and no man shall accept it.

picks.title: The Cry of Libertas
picks.flavour: The cry raised over Caesar's body still carries in the Forum.

picks.title: Philosophy at Tusculum
picks.flavour: Where the Liberators are calm, the consulars follow them into the Curia.

picks.title: The Cap of Liberty
picks.flavour: The felt cap of the freed slave, raised on a spear at the theatre.

power.title: Consult the Fathers
power.flavour: The tubicen calls, the curule chairs are set, and the consulars speak in order.

law.title: Provinces by the Lot
law.flavour: Provinces shall be allotted by lot, as our ancestors allotted them.

picks.title: Auctoritas Patrum
picks.flavour: What the Fathers advise, the magistrates carry out.

picks.title: The Dawn Salutatio
picks.flavour: Clients crowd your door at first light, and their patrons take note.

picks.title: Concordia Ordinum
picks.flavour: Senators and equites, bound by loans and dinners, keep each other's word.

power.title: The Veterans' Oath
power.flavour: The men who swore to guard Caesar's person now swear to avenge him.

law.title: The Exchange of Provinces
law.flavour: Both Gauls for five years, and the Macedonian legions with them.

picks.title: The Star of Caesar
picks.flavour: Seven nights the comet burned, and the camps called it Caesar's soul.

picks.title: Caesar's Chest
picks.flavour: Calpurnia's 4,000 talents sit in your house, and they buy swords.

picks.title: Oath to Caesar's Person
picks.flavour: When the generals waver, the old oath calls them back to the standards.

power.title: Contio at the Rostra
power.flavour: From the ships' beaks you speak, and the Subura answers with one shout.

law.title: The Antonian Land Law
law.flavour: Land for veterans and the poor, measured out by a board of seven.

picks.title: Voice of the Tribes
picks.flavour: Thirty-five tribes vote, and the Senate's decree weighs less than their tablets.

picks.title: Crossroads Collegia
picks.flavour: The guild banquets and street altars turn out a crowd at your word.

picks.title: Bread and Games
picks.flavour: Silver spent in the Circus comes back as cheers at the Rostra.

centreLaws.title: Amnesty and the Acts
centreLaws.flavour: The murderers go unpunished, and every act of Caesar stands as law.

centreLaws.title: Harmony of the Orders
centreLaws.flavour: Senate, equites and plebs each get their share, and the legions their pay.

iron.title: The Ituraean Archers
iron.flavour: Eastern bowmen stand at the Curia doors while the Fathers vote.

iron.title: Decimation at Brundisium
iron.flavour: The ringleaders die before the ranks, and the rest learn obedience.

iron.title: The Cowed Curia
iron.flavour: With veterans at the doors, the Senate's anger rises slowly.

open.title: Free Votes in the Tribes
open.flavour: The ballot urns stand open, and the vote is counted honestly.

open.title: The Right of Appeal
open.flavour: No citizen is beaten or killed without appeal to the people.

open.title: The Tribunes' Bench
open.flavour: Tribunes sit at the Curia door and carry your measures in.

centre.title: The Tellus Compromise
centre.flavour: Hostages exchanged, Brutus dining with Lepidus: the middle way holds.

centre.title: Friend of Both Camps
centre.flavour: Like Atticus, you lend to every side and are trusted by all.

centre.title: Hostages on the Capitol
centre.flavour: Each side holds the other's sons, and laws pass more easily.

iron.title: Veterans Ring the Temple
iron.flavour: Armed veterans stand around the Temple of Tellus while the Senate meets.

iron.title: The Ringleaders Executed
iron.flavour: Centurions named by their men die before the assembled legion.

open.title: Free Speech in the Curia
open.flavour: Any senator may rise and speak, even against the consul.

open.title: Pardon and Recall
open.flavour: Exiles come home, and the angriest men are given a hearing.

egy.title: Alexandrian Grain
egy.flavour: The queen's grain ships reach the Tiber wharves as a gift.

par.title: Peace on the Euphrates
par.flavour: Orodes's envoys swear peace, and the eastern legions can turn west.

gal.title: The Galatian Legion
gal.flavour: Deiotarus sends silver and his legion drilled in the Roman manner.

visions.name: Avenger of Caesar
visions.line: Hold Caesar's legions and provinces, and rule as his true successor.

pillars.text: Keep the Caesarians at 60 or more.

visions.name: Concord after the Ides
visions.line: Keep the amnesty and Caesar's acts together, and stand between the camps.

pillars.text: Raise the Senate to 55 or more.
Bring the Liberatores up to 30 or more.

visions.name: The Republic Restored
visions.line: Bring the Liberators home and give the city back free votes.

pillars.text: Raise the Liberatores to 45 or more.

visions.name: First Man of the Senate
visions.line: Govern with the Fathers, and let their decrees carry your name.

pillars.text: Raise the Senate to 60 or more.

visions.name: The People's Consul
visions.line: Give the plebs land and grain, and rule through the tribes.

pillars.text: Raise the Plebs & Collegia to 70 or more.

combos.name: Veterans on the Land
combos.why: Bind the veterans by oath, then settle them with the land law.

combos.name: Dictatorship Abolished, Senate Restored
combos.why: Ending the dictatorship pleases the Senate, whose answers then hit harder.

combos.name: Iron Consul
combos.why: Caesar's chest pays the legions while decimation makes crackdowns cheap.

lbr.title: The Praetors Write
lbr.question: Consul, will you keep the amnesty, or must Brutus and Cassius flee?
lbr.body: A letter comes from Lanuvium under the seals of Brutus and Cassius. They are still praetors, yet cannot enter Rome. Veterans chalk their names on the walls of the Subura. They ask that the amnesty of 17 March be kept, a guard, and no altar raised to Caesar.

answers.text: Cut the amnesty in bronze and guard their houses
answers.sub: Brutus and Cassius may return; no trial for the Ides.

reasons.lbr: The decree of Tellus stands, and our lives with it.
reasons.sen: Amnesty kept is concord kept; the Curia can breathe.
reasons.cpt: Guards for Caesar's murderers, paid with Caesar's own silver.
reasons.plb: The consul shields the knives that killed our Caesar.
reasons.oct: The heir's vengeance is postponed by the consul's guard.

answers.gripWhy: The conspirators walk freely and speak in the Senate again.

answers.text: Refuse them: Caesar's murderers deserve no guard
answers.sub: No protection; the veterans may do as they please.

reasons.lbr: Refused protection, we must leave Italy or die.
reasons.cpt: Finally the consul names the Ides a crime.
reasons.oct: The assassins are cut loose; vengeance can begin.
reasons.plb: No shield for the knives; the Forum is ours.
reasons.sen: Amnesty broken in a letter; who is safe now?

answers.gripWhy: Your refusal leaves the streets to armed veterans.

answers.text: Refer their plea to the Senate for decree
answers.sub: The consulars decide; you neither shield nor accuse.

reasons.lbr: A hearing before the fathers is better than silence.
reasons.sen: The consul returns a great question to its proper house.
reasons.eqt: Law, not the street, settles it; markets calm.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's killers debated as if they had a case.
reasons.plb: The Senate will shelter its own; the consul hides.

sen.title: The Empty Curia
sen.question: Consul, will you send the veterans away before the Senate meets?
sen.body: You summon the Senate and the benches stand half empty. The consulars have gone to their villas. Cicero writes from Tusculum that no free vote is possible while armed veterans ring the temple steps. Without a quorum no province can be allotted and no act confirmed.

answers.text: Dismiss the guard and summon the Senate freely
answers.sub: Veterans leave the city; the fathers debate without swords.

reasons.sen: No swords at the door: the Senate's authority returns.
reasons.eqt: A free Senate means safe contracts and calm markets.
reasons.lbr: The tyrant's soldiers leave; we may come back.
reasons.cpt: Without the veterans the boni will strip Caesar's men.
reasons.oct: The fathers need the heir less if the consul behaves.

answers.gripWhy: The armed guard leaves and the Senate votes without fear.

answers.text: Keep the veterans and convene the Senate under arms
answers.sub: Guards ring the Curia; senators who stay away are fined.

reasons.sen: An army in Italy against our will: our red line.
reasons.lbr: The next tyrant has shown his face already.
reasons.eqt: Soldiers in the Forum frighten every lender.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's men keep the city; the boni stay quiet.
reasons.oct: Every senator you frighten comes asking for the heir.

answers.gripWhy: Senators summoned and fined under the eyes of soldiers.

answers.text: Carry your laws to the tribes instead
answers.sub: Lucius Antonius brings bills to the assembly; the Senate is bypassed.

reasons.plb: The sovereign people vote, not five hundred old men.
reasons.cpt: The tribes will vote Caesar's men their provinces.
reasons.sen: Our authority ignored as in the days of Clodius.
reasons.eqt: Laws from the street mean debt laws next.
reasons.lbr: Mob-voted laws, the very road of the Gracchi.

answers.gripWhy: The assembly votes openly; no decree stands between.

cpt.title: Lepidus Grows Cold
cpt.question: Consul, will you avenge Caesar, or must his generals look elsewhere?
cpt.body: Lepidus, pontifex maximus, holds the legions of Narbonensis and Nearer Spain. His letters grow shorter. Plancus and Pollio ask the same questions: who confirms Caesar's grants, who punishes the Ides. A military tribune says Caesar's men will follow whoever answers first.

answers.text: Swear vengeance for Caesar before the legion's eagles
answers.sub: Indict the assassins; confirm Lepidus's provinces and priesthood.

reasons.cpt: Vengeance and our commands secured: the consul is ours.
reasons.oct: The heir's cause becomes the consul's cause.
reasons.plb: Caesar's killers named at last before the eagles.
reasons.lbr: A trial for the Ides: the red line crossed.
reasons.sen: The amnesty torn up by an oath in camp.

answers.gripWhy: Indictments sworn in a camp, not voted in a court.

answers.text: Confirm their provinces by Senate decree
answers.sub: Commands made lawful by the fathers; no word of vengeance.

reasons.cpt: Our provinces secure, though Caesar lies unavenged.
reasons.sen: Governors who owe their posts to a decree.
reasons.lbr: Commands by decree, not by sworn vengeance.
reasons.oct: The consul bargains with the Senate over Caesar's blood.
reasons.plb: Provinces for generals, nothing for Caesar's people.

answers.text: Give Caesar's veterans land through the tribes
answers.sub: A land bill at the assembly; generals share the credit.

reasons.cpt: Our soldiers settled, and they remember who led them.
reasons.plb: Land for the poor and the veterans alike.
reasons.eqt: Surveyors on Italian estates; whose land is next?
reasons.sen: Land laws in the tribes, over the Senate's head.
reasons.oct: The veterans' gratitude goes to the consul, not the heir.

oct.title: The Heir's Demand

carrier.name: Gaius Caecina Largus
carrier.role: Agent of the heir in Campania

oct.question: Consul, will you hand over Caesar's money and let the adoption pass?
oct.body: Caesar's heir is selling his own estates to pay the 300-sesterce bequest. He says the consul holds Caesar's chest of 4,000 talents and blocks the curiate law on his adoption. His agents tour Campania. Veterans there drink to the name Caesar, not to yours.

answers.text: Pay out Caesar's chest and pass the curiate law
answers.sub: The heir gets his father's money and his name by law.

reasons.oct: Caesar's money and name: the consul keeps his word.
reasons.plb: The bequest will be paid, every sesterce.
reasons.cpt: A rich boy with Caesar's name courts our veterans.
reasons.sen: One more Caesar with an army's silver.
reasons.egy: A Roman son by law shuts out Caesarion.

answers.text: Send the estate to the praetor's court
answers.sub: Lawyers decide what is Caesar's and what is the state's.

reasons.oct: Years of lawsuits while the veterans forget me.
reasons.eqt: An estate settled by law, the creditors paid first.
reasons.sen: Inheritance belongs to the courts, not the Forum.
reasons.cpt: The boy kept waiting; Caesar's men stay with you.
reasons.plb: The bequest buried in lawyers' wax tablets.

answers.text: Pay the 300 sesterces yourself from the chest
answers.sub: The people get Caesar's gift in your name, not his.

reasons.plb: The bequest paid, and by the consul's own hand.
reasons.oct: My father's money spent to buy the people for him.
reasons.cpt: The consul, not the boy, wears Caesar's generosity.
reasons.eqt: Caesar's chest emptied on the crowd, not on debts.
reasons.sen: Silver for the mob buys a tyrant's following.

plb.title: The Forum Burns
plb.question: Consul, will you feed the city and punish Caesar's killers?
plb.body: Bread costs twice what it did at the Ides. The guilds of the Subura have built altars at the pyre site and stoned your speakers from the Rostra. Lucius Antonius can no longer hold the tribes. The crowd chants for grain, for games, and for the blood of the Ides.

answers.text: Open the granaries and give games in Caesar's name
answers.sub: Grain at the wharves, beasts in the Circus, paid by treasury.

reasons.plb: Bread and the Circus: the consul remembers his people.
reasons.cpt: A fed city does not riot against Caesar's men.
reasons.oct: The consul steals the heir's games and the people's thanks.
reasons.eqt: Treasury silver on the mob means new taxes later.
reasons.sen: The aerarium emptied to please the Subura.

answers.gripWhy: The collegia feast and meet freely again.

answers.text: Raise a column to Caesar, Father of his Country
answers.sub: A marble column at the pyre: PARENTI PATRIAE.

reasons.plb: Caesar honoured where he burned; the altar stands.
reasons.oct: My father honoured as a god in the Forum.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's memory set in stone; the Ides a crime.
reasons.lbr: Honours to Caesar as a god: never.
reasons.sen: A cult of the dead tyrant in the Forum.

answers.text: Close the collegia and clear the Forum by decree
answers.sub: Lictors pull down the altar; the guilds are banned again.

reasons.plb: Our guilds banned, our altar smashed: Clodius's days return.
reasons.sen: Order at last, as the decree of 64 commanded.
reasons.eqt: Shops reopen when the stones stop flying.
reasons.lbr: The mob that burned our doors is broken.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's people beaten for loving Caesar.

answers.gripWhy: Guilds banned and lictors clearing the Forum by force.

eqt.title: The Bankers Close

carrier.name: Decimus Vettienus Rufus
carrier.role: Agent of the Asian tax company

eqt.question: Consul, will you guarantee the contracts, or let the banks shut?
eqt.body: In the basilicas the money-changers have closed their tables. Loans to senators are called in. The Asian company has stopped advancing the tribute. Atticus's friends hear talk of new tables, the cancellation of debts, and of estates of absent Pompeians put up for sale.

answers.text: Swear by edict: no new tables, no confiscations
answers.sub: Debts stand, property is safe, and the tax contracts hold.

reasons.eqt: Our loans and estates are safe; the tables reopen.
reasons.sen: Property guarded, as the boni have always demanded.
reasons.lbr: No confiscations: our families' land stays ours.
reasons.plb: No relief for the poor while bankers sleep soundly.
reasons.cpt: No estates to settle our veterans on.

answers.text: Remit a year's rent for every tenant in Rome
answers.sub: Tenements up to 2,000 sesterces pay nothing for a year.

reasons.plb: A year without the landlord's knock: the consul is ours.
reasons.oct: The consul outbids my father's bequest with rent relief.
reasons.cpt: The city is quiet, and quiet keeps our legions loyal.
reasons.eqt: Rents gone today, debts gone tomorrow: our red line.
reasons.sen: The property of the boni given to the mob.

answers.text: Pledge Egypt's tribute to the bankers' company
answers.sub: Caesar's client queen pays; the publicani advance silver now.

reasons.eqt: Egyptian gold as security: we can lend again.
reasons.cpt: The legions get paid, whoever's gold it is.
reasons.egy: My kingdom's revenue pawned to Roman usurers without my leave.
reasons.sen: The consul trades kingdoms like a Hellenistic king.
reasons.plb: Silver for bankers, while the grain stays dear.

egy.title: The Queen Will Sail
egy.question: Consul, will you name Caesarion Caesar's son before the queen sails?
egy.body: At Caesar's villa across the Tiber the queen's household packs; her ships wait at Ostia. Her steward says she leaves this month. She asks one thing: that the Senate hear the consul name Caesarion son of Caesar. Egypt's grain, treasury and the legions in Alexandria wait on the answer.

answers.text: Name Caesarion Caesar's son before the Senate
answers.sub: The boy declared Caesar's blood; the queen bound to you.

reasons.egy: My son named by Caesar's consul: Egypt is yours.
reasons.oct: A rival son of Caesar raised against my adoption.
reasons.cpt: Egypt's gold and legions for Caesar's party.
reasons.sen: An Egyptian bastard as Caesar's son? Shame on the Curia.
reasons.plb: The foreign queen's boy, honoured before the bequest.

answers.text: Renew her title as friend and ally of Rome
answers.sub: Her throne is confirmed; her son is not mentioned.

reasons.egy: Allied, but my son ignored: half a promise.
reasons.sen: The Senate's old style with clients: firm and correct.
reasons.oct: No rival son spoken of in the Curia.
reasons.eqt: Egypt's trade stays open and its debts repayable.

answers.text: Buy her Alexandrian grain for Rome at full price
answers.sub: The queen's ships unload at Ostia; the plebs eat.

reasons.egy: Roman silver for our grain; a fair friend.
reasons.plb: Egyptian wheat on the Tiber wharves, cheap again.
reasons.eqt: Treasury silver to a queen, not to our creditors.
reasons.sen: Paying a client for what she owes as tribute.

par.title: The Euphrates Envoy

carrier.name: Mithrenes
carrier.role: Envoy of the King of Kings

par.question: Consul, will you call off Caesar's Parthian war for good?
par.body: An envoy of Orodes comes by way of Syria, where Caecilius Bassus holds out at Apamea with Parthian horse beside him. Six legions still wait in Macedonia for Caesar's war. The King of Kings offers peace on the river, if no Roman avenger crosses it.

answers.text: Swear peace on the Euphrates by Senate decree
answers.sub: Caesar's war cancelled; the Senate receives the envoys formally.

reasons.par: No avenger on the river: the King of Kings is content.
reasons.sen: War and peace decided in the Curia, as of old.
reasons.eqt: Peace in the East means Asia's tribute flows again.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's war, its plunder and commands, thrown away.
reasons.egy: Parthia unchecked on Syria's border, close to Egypt.

answers.text: Order the Macedonian legions east toward Syria
answers.sub: Caesar's war resumes against Bassus and the Parthian horse.

reasons.par: The Caesarian avenger marches, as the king feared.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's war, Caesar's spoils, our commands.
reasons.egy: Roman legions in Syria shield Egypt from Parthia.
reasons.eqt: War in the East stops every tax payment.
reasons.sen: A war voted by no one in the Curia.

answers.text: Leave Syria to Cassius and the Senate's men
answers.sub: No legions east; the eastern provinces govern themselves.

reasons.par: Romans who fight each other are good neighbours.
reasons.lbr: Syria left to Cassius: the East becomes our base.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's murderers handed the eastern legions.
reasons.egy: Cassius at our border, and no Caesarian to stop him.
reasons.oct: The East given to the knives of the Ides.

gal.title: The King's Bond

carrier.name: Toutobocio
carrier.role: Envoy of the King of Galatia

gal.question: Consul, will you sign the Armenian decree, or lose the king's legion?
gal.body: Envoys from Galatia remind you of the bond for 10 million sesterces that Fulvia accepted. Lesser Armenia is still not returned to Deiotarus. The old king keeps a legion drilled in the Roman fashion, and the Roman commanders in Asia would gladly take it.

answers.text: Publish the decree as found in Caesar's papers
answers.sub: Caesar's 'own' act restores Lesser Armenia; the bond is paid.

reasons.gal: Lesser Armenia returned, the bond honoured: the king is yours.
reasons.cpt: A client king bound to Caesar's acts.
reasons.eqt: The bond paid, the roads of Anatolia quiet.
reasons.sen: Another act of Caesar no one ever saw.
reasons.lbr: Forged acts of the tyrant, sold for silver.

answers.gripWhy: Law made by your seal alone, from a dead man's notes.

answers.text: Put the king's claim before the Senate
answers.sub: The consulars weigh it; the king waits months.

reasons.gal: Months of debate while Roman generals court my legion.
reasons.sen: A client's claim heard in the proper house.
reasons.eqt: A lawful decree is a safer contract.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's judgement on Deiotarus reopened by the boni.

answers.text: Return the bond: no law is sold for silver
answers.sub: Fulvia returns the 10 million; Armenia stays as Caesar left it.

reasons.gal: Silver returned, land refused: the king is insulted.
reasons.lbr: A consul who will not sell the Republic's laws.
reasons.sen: Clean hands, at last, on Caesar's papers.
reasons.eqt: A broken bargain worries every lender in Rome.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's ruling stands, but the party loses the silver.

elections.title: The Tribunes' Comitia
elections.question: Consul, will you let the tribes elect a tribune freely?
elections.body: Helvius Cinna, torn apart by the funeral crowd, leaves a tribune's seat empty. The tribes gather at the Saepta to fill it. Caesar's heir backs a candidate of his own, and the plebs cheer the name. As augur, you may watch the sky and see bad omens.

answers.text: Open the Saepta and let the tribes vote
answers.sub: The plebs fill Cinna's seat with whomever they choose.

reasons.plb: The tribes choose their own tribune, as is right.
reasons.oct: My candidate can win in an open vote.
reasons.lbr: A free vote, even in this city of veterans.
reasons.cpt: A tribune of the heir could veto Caesar's acts.
reasons.sen: One more demagogue on the tribunes' bench.

answers.gripWhy: A free vote at the Saepta, no soldiers near.

answers.text: Watch the sky as augur and postpone the vote
answers.sub: Bad omens declared; the comitia dissolve until further notice.

reasons.plb: The augur's trick, used against the people's vote.
reasons.oct: The consul blocks my candidate with birds and thunder.
reasons.sen: The auspices respected, the mob sent home.
reasons.cpt: No heir's tribune to trouble Caesar's men.
reasons.eqt: No new tribune means no new debt bill.

answers.gripWhy: The vote suspended by your word as augur.

answers.text: March the veterans into the Saepta to vote
answers.sub: Caesar's soldiers fill the pens; your man takes the seat.

reasons.cpt: Caesar's soldiers choose the tribune; the party holds.
reasons.oct: The veterans voted for the consul, not for me.
reasons.plb: Soldiers in our voting pens: the tribunate stolen.
reasons.sen: Armed men at the comitia: the end of the Republic.
reasons.lbr: The tyrant's method, in the tyrant's place.

answers.gripWhy: Armed men fill the voting pens under your orders.

elections.title: The Praetorian Comitia
elections.question: Consul, will you let the centuries choose next year's magistrates?
elections.body: Caesar named the magistrates for two years ahead before he died. Now the Campus Martius waits for the centuries to vote the praetors and aediles of 43. Candidates crowd the consul's door at dawn. A free vote would return names the dictator never chose.

answers.text: Let the centuries vote freely on the Campus
answers.sub: Any citizen may stand; Caesar's list is set aside.

reasons.lbr: Yearly magistrates, freely chosen: the Republic breathes.
reasons.sen: The centuries vote, as the ancestors ordained.
reasons.plb: The people's vote, at least, still counts for something.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's appointments discarded; our men lose their offices.
reasons.oct: Free elections favour the old houses, not Caesar's son.

answers.gripWhy: Free comitia on the Campus, with open candidacies.

answers.text: Publish Caesar's list and declare them elected
answers.sub: Caesar's designations stand; the centuries only cheer.

reasons.cpt: Caesar's choices honoured: our men take their offices.
reasons.oct: My father's will in government as in property.
reasons.lbr: Magistrates named by a dead tyrant: no Republic at all.
reasons.sen: The comitia made a ceremony, as under the dictator.
reasons.plb: The people's vote reduced to a show.

answers.gripWhy: Elections replaced by a dead man's list.

answers.text: Ask the Senate to postpone the comitia
answers.sub: A decree delays the vote until the city is calm.

reasons.sen: The fathers decide when Rome is fit to vote.
reasons.eqt: No campaign bribes, no riots on the Campus.
reasons.cpt: Our designated men keep their places a while.
reasons.lbr: Postponement serves the consul who holds the papers.
reasons.plb: Our votes delayed again by old men in the Curia.

answers.gripWhy: The vote postponed by decree under your presidency.

elections.title: The Vote on Gaul
elections.question: Consul, will you put your provinces law before the tribes?
elections.body: Your bill gives you Cisalpine and Transalpine Gaul for five years with the Macedonian legions. Decimus Brutus holds Cisalpine Gaul now by Caesar's grant. The Senate refuses to decree it. The tribes can pass it, if the bill stands three market days before them.

answers.text: Post the bill for three market days, then vote
answers.sub: The trinundinum is kept; the tribes vote openly.

reasons.plb: The tribes decide the consul's province themselves.
reasons.sen: At least the forms of the ancestors are kept.
reasons.cpt: Gaul and the legions in a Caesarian's hands.
reasons.lbr: Decimus's province taken by vote of the mob.
reasons.eqt: Five years of armies near Italy worry the markets.

answers.gripWhy: A lawful public vote after full notice.

answers.text: Pass it in one day under armed guard
answers.sub: Veterans hold the Forum; the vote is done by noon.

reasons.cpt: Gaul secured fast, before the Senate can scheme.
reasons.plb: A Caesarian in Gaul suits the Forum.
reasons.oct: The consul takes Caesar's armies for himself.
reasons.sen: An army in Italy and a law passed by swords.
reasons.lbr: The new tyrant takes Caesar's own road, Gaul first.

answers.gripWhy: A law passed under soldiers' eyes in one day.

answers.text: Withdraw the bill; leave Decimus his province
answers.sub: Caesar's grant to Decimus stands; you take Macedonia only.

reasons.lbr: Decimus keeps Cisalpine Gaul; Italy stays unguarded by tyrants.
reasons.sen: The consul yields to the Senate's allotment.
reasons.oct: The consul stays weak; the heir has room to rise.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's murderer guards the gate of Italy.
reasons.plb: The consul backs down before the assassins.

history.title: Lepidus in the Forum
history.question: Consul, my legion holds the Forum. Will you let me storm the Capitol?
history.body: Dawn, 16 March. Lepidus has marched his legion from the Tiber Island into the Forum. Brutus, Cassius and their friends hold the Capitol behind Decimus Brutus's gladiators. Veterans shout for vengeance at the foot of the hill. Senators bar their doors.

answers.text: Storm the Capitol and avenge Caesar today
answers.sub: The legion climbs the Clivus; the assassins die or flee.

reasons.cpt: Vengeance now, and the legion's glory is ours.
reasons.oct: My father's murderers pay in blood at once.
reasons.plb: The crowd wants the killers dragged down the steps.
reasons.lbr: Your soldiers mean our throats on the sacred hill.
reasons.sen: Blood on Jupiter's steps; you are already a tyrant.
reasons.eqt: Civil war in the city; the banks shut tonight.

answers.gripWhy: Soldiers storm the citadel inside the sacred boundary.

answers.text: Send your son up the hill as hostage
answers.sub: Parley as equals; the assassins come down unharmed.

reasons.lbr: A consul's son in our hands; we can come down.
reasons.sen: Talk instead of swords; the Senate can meet again.
reasons.eqt: No sack of the city; our strongrooms stay full.
reasons.cpt: You hand Caesar's killers a hostage instead of a sword.
reasons.plb: The murderers walk free while Caesar lies unburned.
reasons.oct: The consul bargains with my father's killers.

answers.gripWhy: Parley with armed men replaces the legion's assault.

answers.text: Summon the Senate to the Temple of Tellus
answers.sub: Let the fathers decide, with veterans ringing the temple.

reasons.sen: The Senate's authority decides, not a legion's swords.
reasons.eqt: Order and debate; credit holds for another day.
reasons.lbr: Debate gives our friends a voice and us time.
reasons.cpt: Talk wastes the hour while our legion stands ready.
reasons.oct: Senators who sheltered the killers will now judge them.

answers.gripWhy: Power passes from the legion back to the Curia.

history.history: In history: Antonius held Lepidus back, sent his young son up the Capitol as a hostage, and called the Senate to meet in the Temple of Tellus.

history.title: Amnesty at Tellus
history.question: Consul, the fathers await your motion. What will you propose on the assassins?
history.body: 17 March, Temple of Tellus. Veterans crowd the steps and shout for the assassins' heads. Cicero pleads for an amnesty, as Athens once forgave its citizens. Some senators move honours for the tyrannicides. Caesar's officers fear losing their posts if Caesar was a tyrant.

answers.text: Amnesty for the assassins, all Caesar's acts confirmed
answers.sub: No honours, no trials; every appointment and law stands.

reasons.sen: Cicero's concord: the fathers keep peace and their posts.
reasons.eqt: Contracts and appointments stand; credit can breathe again.
reasons.lbr: We live, though no one calls us liberators.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's acts stand, so our provinces and priesthoods stand.
reasons.plb: The killers of our Caesar go home to dinner.
reasons.oct: My father's murderers pardoned before his body is cold.

answers.gripWhy: A pardon freely voted in the Senate.

answers.text: Honour them as tyrannicides who freed Rome
answers.sub: Caesar declared a tyrant; his acts open to repeal.

reasons.lbr: The Ides made glorious, as our ancestor drove out kings.
reasons.sen: The fathers win back the power one man took.
reasons.par: Caesar's Parthian war dies with his acts.
reasons.cpt: Our commands fall with his acts; this means war.
reasons.plb: You spit on Caesar and his gifts to us.
reasons.oct: My adoption and inheritance hang on Caesar's acts.

answers.gripWhy: The free Republic proclaimed; one man's rule repudiated.

answers.text: Refuse amnesty and charge the assassins with murder
answers.sub: A court for the killers; the veterans guard the trial.

reasons.cpt: Caesar's killers before a court of his own men.
reasons.oct: Vengeance for my father, done under the law's name.
reasons.plb: Justice for Caesar, as the crowd demands it.
reasons.lbr: A trial means death; we will have to fight.
reasons.sen: The fathers sat in fear; now they will be judged.
reasons.eqt: Trials mean confiscations, and confiscations reach our houses.

answers.gripWhy: Veterans guard prosecutions of the city's first men.

history.history: In history: on Cicero's plea the Senate granted the assassins impunity without honours and confirmed all Caesar's acts; Brutus and Cassius dined with Lepidus and Antonius.

history.title: The Pyre in the Forum
history.question: The crowd carries torches to the assassins' houses. Will you stop them?
history.body: 20 March. After your laudatio and the bloodied toga, the crowd burned Caesar's body in the Forum on benches and magistrates' chairs. A mob killed a tribune, mistaking him for a conspirator. Torches now move toward the assassins' houses.

answers.text: Let the people mourn Caesar their own way
answers.sub: No soldiers in the streets; the crowd rules the night.

reasons.plb: The people burn their Caesar and punish his killers.
reasons.oct: Rome's grief for my father is plain to all.
reasons.cpt: The killers learn the city will never forgive them.
reasons.lbr: The mob hunts us through the streets tonight.
reasons.sen: The consul hands the city to arsonists.
reasons.eqt: Fire spreads; our warehouses burn with their houses.

answers.gripWhy: The crowd is left free in the streets.

answers.text: Guard the houses of the men who freed Rome
answers.sub: Lepidus's soldiers hold the streets; the crowd is driven back.

reasons.lbr: The consul protects Rome's liberators; we may stay.
reasons.sen: The amnesty means something if the consul enforces it.
reasons.eqt: Soldiers stop the fire before it reaches the banks.
reasons.plb: Soldiers drive us from Caesar's pyre to save his murderers.
reasons.cpt: Our legion guarding Caesar's killers? The men will not bear it.
reasons.oct: The consul shields my father's murderers with Caesar's troops.

answers.gripWhy: Soldiers clear the Forum of mourners by force.

history.history: In history: the crowd burned the body in the Forum, killed a tribune by mistake and attacked the conspirators' houses, and the consul let the fury run.

history.title: Brutus Leaves the City
history.question: The urban praetor asks leave to be absent. Will you grant it?
history.body: April. Brutus and Cassius, unsafe in a city where veterans roam, have gone to Lanuvium. They are still praetors. The law lets the urban praetor leave Rome for only ten days. Brutus asks you for a dispensation from the Senate.

answers.text: Win Brutus his dispensation; keep his office safe
answers.sub: The Senate excuses his absence; he stays praetor in law.

reasons.lbr: Brutus keeps his rank and the amnesty keeps its word.
reasons.sen: The fathers are consulted and the law bent gently.
reasons.par: Rome's strong men quarrel; the Euphrates stays quiet.
reasons.plb: The murderer keeps his chair while we wait for grain.
reasons.cpt: You keep Caesar's killers in high office for nothing.
reasons.oct: My father's assassin holds the city's praetorship still.

answers.gripWhy: A lawful dispensation granted by free Senate vote.

answers.text: Let the tribes strip the absent praetors of office
answers.sub: Lucius Antonius brings a plebiscite; Brutus and Cassius lose their chairs.

reasons.plb: The people's vote throws Caesar's killers out of office.
reasons.cpt: No praetorships for assassins; the amnesty spared only lives.
reasons.oct: My father's killers lose their dignity at least.
reasons.lbr: The plebs vote away our offices; next comes exile.
reasons.sen: The tribes override the Senate's own magistrates.
reasons.eqt: Plebiscites against nobles frighten every lender in Rome.

answers.gripWhy: Magistrates removed by a crowd's vote under the consul's eye.

history.history: In history: Brutus and Cassius left Rome for Lanuvium in April, and the consul had the Senate excuse Brutus's absence beyond the ten days the law allowed.

history.title: The Heir in Campania
history.question: The boy dines with Balbus and the consuls-designate. What will you do about him?
history.body: April. Gaius Octavius landed from Apollonia and now calls himself Caesar. Near Puteoli he has met Balbus, Caesar's agent, and Hirtius and Pansa, consuls for next year. Cicero dined with him too. The veterans in Campania already say his name.

answers.text: Ignore the boy; Caesar's legions and papers are yours
answers.sub: You act as Caesar's true successor and keep his chest.

reasons.cpt: One Caesarian chief, not two; the generals know you.
reasons.egy: One strong Caesarian in Rome is what the queen needs.
reasons.gal: Caesar's papers stay with you; my decree can still be bought.
reasons.eqt: Caesar's chest stays in steady hands, not a boy's.
reasons.oct: The consul treats Caesar's son as a boy beneath notice.
reasons.plb: The heir would pay the bequest; you keep the money.

answers.text: Pay Caesar's 300 sesterces yourself from his chest
answers.sub: You take the people's thanks before the heir can.

reasons.plb: Three hundred a head, paid by the consul at once.
reasons.cpt: The consul, not the boy, wins Caesar's people.
reasons.oct: You spend my inheritance to buy my father's people.
reasons.eqt: The chest empties on gifts while loans go unpaid.
reasons.sen: Public bribery with a dead man's money.

history.history: In history: the consul paid the heir no heed in April; Octavius kept Hirtius, Pansa and Balbus close and began courting Cicero and the veterans.

history.title: Omens over the Assembly
history.question: Consulars report ill omens to void the vote. Will you hold it?
history.body: 2 June. Your law to take both Gauls for five years, with the Macedonian army, goes to the tribes. Veterans fill the Forum. The Senate stays away. Consulars send word they have watched the sky and seen ill omens. You are an augur yourself.

answers.text: Put the law to the tribes; the people decide
answers.sub: The vote goes ahead; the tribes give you the Gauls.

reasons.plb: The sovereign people vote, whatever the consulars mutter.
reasons.cpt: Five years in Gaul with an army: a Caesarian bulwark.
reasons.lbr: The consul takes Decimus's province by a street vote.
reasons.sen: The auspices mocked and the Senate's allotment overthrown.
reasons.eqt: Five years of armies in Gaul cost someone money.
reasons.oct: The consul arms himself with Caesar's legions, not me.

answers.gripWhy: Veterans stand over the voters in the Forum.

answers.text: Ring the Forum with veterans and pass it
answers.sub: Armed men at every gangway; no tribune dares veto.

reasons.cpt: Caesar's way: soldiers secure what laws only promise.
reasons.oct: The consul's swords, not Caesar's heir, rule the Forum.
reasons.plb: Soldiers at the voting gangways insult free citizens.
reasons.sen: Armed men in an assembly: Caesar's tyranny again.
reasons.lbr: The consul shows us the next dictator's face.

answers.gripWhy: Soldiers in the voting enclosure overawe the tribes.

answers.text: Adjourn; the auspices bind even a consul
answers.sub: The bill waits; the Senate allots the provinces by lot.

reasons.sen: The mos maiorum honoured; the Senate keeps its provinces.
reasons.eqt: No armies in Gaul for five years; taxes stay low.
reasons.lbr: Decimus keeps Cisalpine Gaul by Caesar's own grant.
reasons.cpt: Without the Gauls the consul has no army near Rome.
reasons.plb: The consulars' sky-watching cheats the people's vote again.

answers.gripWhy: The consul yields to the augurs and the Senate.

history.history: In history: on 2 June, with veterans cowing the Senate, the tribal assembly passed the lex de permutatione provinciarum, giving the consul both Gauls for five years.

history.title: Caesar's Star
history.question: The people call the comet Caesar's soul. Will you proclaim him a god?
history.body: Late July. At Octavian's games for Caesar's victories a comet blazes for seven days, bright even at the eleventh hour. The crowd calls it Caesar's soul among the gods. Octavian has set a star on his father's statue. The priests await your word.

answers.text: Forbid the cult; Caesar was a man, not god
answers.sub: No altars, no star; the augurs record a comet.

reasons.lbr: No god-kings in Rome; the Ides stand justified.
reasons.sen: No new cult raised by street crowds and a boy.
reasons.plb: You forbid us to honour Caesar under his own star.
reasons.oct: My father's star denied by the man he raised.
reasons.cpt: Insulting Caesar's divinity insults every man who served him.
reasons.egy: The queen's son is born of a god or nothing.

answers.gripWhy: Altars pulled down and a popular cult forbidden.

answers.text: Decree nothing; leave the sign to the augurs
answers.sub: No cult, no ban; the omen stays the heir's to use.

reasons.sen: The priests, not the crowd, read the gods' signs.
reasons.eqt: Calm in the city and no new festival costs.
reasons.oct: Your silence leaves Caesar's star to me alone.
reasons.plb: The consul shrugs while Caesar's soul shines over us.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's own colleague will not honour his star.

answers.text: Let the crossroads raise altars to Caesar's star
answers.sub: The colleges build shrines; the Lares festivals honour Caesar.

reasons.plb: Our crossroads shrines, our Caesar, our festival.
reasons.oct: The people worship my father; my name grows with it.
reasons.egy: Caesar a god makes Caesarion a god's son.
reasons.sen: Colleges the Senate banned, revived around a dead dictator.
reasons.lbr: Altars to the tyrant at every crossroads.
reasons.eqt: The colleges armed again; Clodius's gangs return.

answers.gripWhy: The colleges freely revived and the crossroads left to them.

history.history: In history: a comet shone seven days during Octavian's games; the people hailed it as Caesar's soul, Octavian set a star on his statue, and the consul stayed silent.

history.title: Copies of the Philippic
history.question: Copies of Cicero's speech sell in the Argiletum. Will you stop them?
history.body: 2 September. Cicero spoke against your use of Caesar's papers, offering friendship if you govern by the laws. Copyists are already at work. Booksellers in the Argiletum sell the speech by the roll. Senators read it aloud at dinner.

answers.text: Let it circulate; write your answer at Tibur
answers.sub: Free speech for all; you reply with words, not men.

reasons.sen: Senate debate stays free; Cicero is answered, not silenced.
reasons.lbr: A consul who suffers free speech is no tyrant yet.
reasons.eqt: Words, not swords; business carries on.
reasons.cpt: Cicero mocks Caesar's acts and the consul debates him?
reasons.plb: Speeches in villas, while we wait for land.

answers.gripWhy: Free circulation of an attack on the consul.

answers.text: Seize the rolls and close the copyists' shops
answers.sub: Lictors in the Argiletum; booksellers fined and rolls burned.

reasons.cpt: Insults to Caesar's acts deserve the fire.
reasons.plb: Let the old orator's lies feed the fire.
reasons.oct: Burning a consular's speech shames Caesar's party, my party.
reasons.sen: Censorship of a consular's speech: the old tyranny returns.
reasons.lbr: First Cicero's books burn, then Cicero, then us.
reasons.eqt: Shops closed and booksellers fined; who is next?

answers.gripWhy: Lictors seize and burn a consular's published speech.

answers.text: Move a Senate censure of Cicero for slander
answers.sub: The fathers vote; Calenus leads your friends against him.

reasons.cpt: Make the Senate itself silence Caesar's enemy.
reasons.eqt: A vote in the Curia, not a riot in the streets.
reasons.sen: The fathers forced to condemn their own leading voice.
reasons.lbr: The Senate turned against its last free speaker.
reasons.oct: You spend the Senate's goodwill; I will collect it.

answers.gripWhy: A Senate vote to punish a speech.

history.history: In history: Cicero's First Philippic circulated freely; the consul withdrew to Tibur for over two weeks and answered on 19 September with a furious invective.

history.title: The Road to Brundisium
history.question: Four Macedonian legions land at Brundisium. Will you go to them yourself?
history.body: 9 October. Four legions from Macedonia are landing at Brundisium. Octavian's agents are already among them with silver. Leaving now means leaving Rome to the heir and to Cicero. Fulvia offers to come with you.

answers.text: Ride to Brundisium and take the legions in hand
answers.sub: A general's place is with his army, not the Rostra.

reasons.cpt: The legions want their general, and so do we.
reasons.oct: Your absence leaves Rome's veterans and Forum to me.
reasons.plb: The consul leaves the city for his soldiers.
reasons.sen: The consul goes to fetch an army against us.
reasons.eqt: Four more legions to pay from a drained treasury.

answers.gripWhy: The consul takes personal command of an army in Italy.

answers.text: Stay in Rome; send your brother Gaius south
answers.sub: You hold the Forum; your brother greets the army.

reasons.plb: The consul stays with the people, not the camps.
reasons.sen: No army marching on the city behind its consul.
reasons.eqt: Fewer soldiers near Rome means fewer requisitions.
reasons.oct: A brother's word will not hold legions against my silver.
reasons.cpt: Legions follow a general, not a praetor brother.

answers.text: Ask the Senate to order the legions to Gaul
answers.sub: The army moves by decree; the fathers share the blame.

reasons.sen: The legions move by the Senate's decree, as law requires.
reasons.eqt: Lawful orders keep soldiers from plundering the roads.
reasons.cpt: A Caesarian army taking orders from Cicero's Senate?
reasons.oct: The Senate becomes your partner, not mine.
reasons.plb: Soldiers marched off by the fathers, not the people.

answers.gripWhy: The army placed under the Senate's lawful authority.

history.history: In history: the consul rode to Brundisium, offered 100 denarii a man, was jeered, and executed centurions and soldiers named as ringleaders.

history.title: The Heir Takes the Rostra
history.question: Caesar's heir speaks against you from the Rostra. How will you answer?
history.body: November. Octavian has bought some 3,000 of Caesar's veterans at 500 denarii a head. He holds the Forum and a tribune has given him the Rostra. He swears to win his father's honours, pointing at Caesar's statue. Many veterans murmur they will not fight a Caesarian consul.

answers.text: Hold your own contio and outshout the boy
answers.sub: Your friends give you the Rostra next morning.

reasons.plb: Two Caesarians court the Forum; the people choose.
reasons.cpt: The consul fights the boy for the crowd and wins.
reasons.oct: You drown my speech with hired cheers.
reasons.sen: Rival mobs in the Forum, as in Clodius's day.
reasons.eqt: Shouting crowds close the shops along the Sacred Way.

answers.gripWhy: Rival speeches before a free crowd.

answers.text: Remind the veterans: Caesar's men don't fight Caesar's men
answers.sub: Your letters reach the camps; the veterans drift away.

reasons.cpt: Caesarians stand together under Caesar's own consul.
reasons.plb: No soldiers fighting in the Forum; the plebs approve.
reasons.oct: My veterans leave me at Caesar's own name.
reasons.sen: The fathers hoped the two Caesarians would destroy each other.
reasons.lbr: A united Caesarian army is our death sentence.

answers.text: Call the Senate: no private citizen may raise legions
answers.sub: You ask the fathers to condemn the heir's private army.

reasons.sen: The Senate alone may arm men; the law is plain.
reasons.eqt: A private army near Rome threatens every estate.
reasons.oct: You would brand Caesar's son a rebel in the Curia.
reasons.cpt: Caesarians sending Caesar's heir to the Senate's judgment?
reasons.plb: The boy pays our bequest; you call him outlaw.

answers.gripWhy: Senate condemnation of an armed private citizen.

history.history: In history: most veterans refused to fight a Caesarian consul; Octavian spoke from the Rostra, then withdrew to Arretium with those who stayed.

history.title: Decimus Praised
history.question: The Senate praises Decimus and your deserters. How will you answer?
history.body: 20 December. On Cicero's motion the Senate has praised Decimus Brutus for holding Cisalpine Gaul against you. It commends the Martia, the Fourth and Octavian. Your consulship ends in eleven days. Your lines close on Mutina in the snow.

answers.text: Declare the decree void and tighten the siege
answers.sub: You hold Gaul by the people's law, not the Senate's whim.

reasons.cpt: A Caesarian holds his province by law and by legions.
reasons.plb: The people gave you Gaul; the Senate cannot take it.
reasons.egy: A Caesarian who will not bow to the assassins' friends.
reasons.oct: Your defiance makes me the Senate's champion.
reasons.sen: The consul defies a decree of the Senate in arms.
reasons.lbr: Decimus starves while the consul mocks the fathers.

answers.gripWhy: A senatus consultum defied by an army in the field.

answers.text: All commanders disarm: you, Decimus, Brutus, Cassius
answers.sub: Every army returns to the Republic; free elections in spring.

reasons.sen: Every army laid before the Senate: the Republic restored.
reasons.lbr: The free Republic's peace, if the tyrant's heir disarms.
reasons.eqt: Peace means tribute flows and loans are repaid.
reasons.cpt: You would throw away the legions that protect us all.
reasons.oct: Disarm me too and Caesar stays unavenged.

answers.gripWhy: Armies offered back to the Senate and the people.

history.history: In history: on Cicero's motion the Senate praised Decimus Brutus on 20 December, and the consul's army closed in on Mutina regardless.

history.title: The New Consuls
history.question: The new consuls open the war debate. How will you meet it?
history.body: 1 January 43. Hirtius and Pansa take the fasces. You are proconsul now, and cannot summon the Senate. Cicero moves war and honours for Octavian. Fufius Calenus can stretch the debate for days. Piso offers to carry terms.

answers.text: Have Calenus win an embassy, not a war
answers.sub: Four days of debate; three consulars carry the Senate's terms.

reasons.sen: Envoys before war: the mos maiorum observed.
reasons.eqt: An embassy means months more of peace and tribute.
reasons.cpt: Time for Lepidus and Plancus to weigh their choice.
reasons.oct: Delay starves my legions of a war to win.
reasons.lbr: Decimus starves longer while the envoys travel.

answers.gripWhy: Decision left to free Senate debate and negotiation.

answers.text: Send agents to the contio: the plebs want peace
answers.sub: Grain and land promised to a city tired of war.

reasons.plb: Peace and grain, not Cicero's war for nobles.
reasons.cpt: The city's mood ties the new consuls' hands.
reasons.eqt: Promises of land mean someone's estate pays.
reasons.sen: Agitators set the crowd against the Senate's war.
reasons.oct: My veterans hear the city does not want me.

answers.gripWhy: Free agitation in the Forum against a war vote.

answers.text: Swear to the laws: amnesty for all, including you
answers.sub: You offer the free Republic's terms: no proscriptions, no tyrants.

reasons.lbr: If the proconsul swears to libertas, Decimus may live.
reasons.sen: A former consul submitting to the laws is welcome.
reasons.par: Rome's quarrels settled by oaths, not Caesar's legions.
reasons.cpt: You beg for pardon like a defeated Pompeian.
reasons.oct: An amnesty for you leaves me no enemy to beat.

answers.gripWhy: A pledge of law and pardon over arms.

history.history: In history: after four days of debate the Senate gave Octavian a seat and propraetorian imperium, and sent three consulars to order the former consul out of Cisalpine Gaul.

situations.title: The Body of Caesar
situations.question: Consul, how will you have Caesar carried to his pyre?
situations.body: Caesar lies at his house on the Sacred Way. Piso holds the will and the Senate's grant of a public funeral. The tribunes say the Forum is filling. Veterans stand armed in the crowd. The Liberators watch from behind barred doors.

answers.text: A quiet rite at the Julian tomb.
answers.sub: Family mourners, ten tibicines, no speech, the Forum kept calm.

reasons.sen: A quiet burial keeps the Forum calm and the Senate safe.
reasons.lbr: No crowd, no speech: the Ides may yet be forgiven.
reasons.eqt: Peace in the streets keeps the banks open.
reasons.plb: The people are denied Caesar's farewell and his will.
reasons.cpt: Caesar buried like a private man is an insult.
reasons.oct: His father hidden away, his inheritance unread.

answers.text: Give the laudatio yourself and read the will.
answers.sub: The 300 sesterces and the gardens announced from the Rostra.

reasons.cpt: The consul speaks for Caesar; his acts and men stand.
reasons.plb: Three hundred sesterces each and Caesar's gardens are ours.
reasons.oct: The will read aloud names him heir before all Rome.
reasons.lbr: Every line of praise is a charge against the Ides.
reasons.sen: A consul's laudatio stirs a crowd the Senate cannot rule.
reasons.eqt: A roused Forum is bad for credit.

answers.text: Raise the wax image with its 23 wounds.
answers.sub: The bloodied toga on a spear; the crowd decides the rest.

reasons.plb: They see his wounds and know who made them.
reasons.cpt: The veterans' fury serves the cause of vengeance.
reasons.lbr: The crowd will come to their doors with torches.
reasons.sen: A mob shown a corpse is a mob unleashed.
reasons.eqt: Burning houses mean burned contracts and fled debtors.

situations.title: The Men from the Capitol
situations.question: Consul, will you guard the men who killed Caesar, or arrest them?
situations.body: The amnesty holds. Your son and Lepidus's son sit on the Capitol as hostages. Brutus and Cassius have come down and ask for a guard and a safe house in Rome. Lepidus says the veterans will kill them first. He offers his legion for the arrest.

answers.text: Give them lictors and the amnesty's protection.
answers.sub: Praetors keep their offices; your guards stand at their doors.

reasons.lbr: Lictors at the door and offices kept: the amnesty is real.
reasons.sen: The Senate's decree of 17 March is obeyed.
reasons.eqt: Order kept, and no new confiscations begun.
reasons.cpt: Guarding Caesar's killers shames every man who served him.
reasons.plb: Their consul protects the murderers of their Caesar.
reasons.oct: His father's killers walk Rome under a guard of honour.

answers.gripWhy: The amnesty is honoured; no one is seized for the Ides.

answers.text: Let Lepidus's legion arrest them for trial.
answers.sub: Brutus and Cassius held under guard; the amnesty broken.

reasons.cpt: Lepidus's legion acts at last; Caesar's blood is answered.
reasons.plb: The murderers in chains, as the Forum demands.
reasons.oct: Vengeance begun, though by another man's hand.
reasons.lbr: The amnesty was a trap; arrest means death.
reasons.sen: A legion seizes praetors against the Senate's decree.
reasons.eqt: Civil war in the city stops every payment.

answers.gripWhy: Praetors in chains by a legion's hand, against the decree.

situations.title: Caesar's Notebooks
situations.question: Consul, will you publish only what Caesar signed, or what you find?
situations.body: Caesar's notebooks lie in your house, with 4,000 talents Calpurnia sent by night. The Senate confirmed his acts, signed and planned. Clients queue at your door: a city wants its tribute lifted, an exile his return. Caesar's secretary holds the pen and knows his hand.

answers.text: Publish only the acts Caesar signed and sealed.
answers.sub: No dead man legislates; unsigned memoranda are sealed away.

reasons.lbr: The tyrant's will ends with his death.
reasons.sen: No forged acts; the Senate's confirmation means what it says.
reasons.eqt: Known laws, known taxes, safe contracts.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's unfinished plans for his friends are thrown away.
reasons.gal: Deiotarus's lands stay lost without a new decree.

answers.text: Find what Caesar 'meant' for those who ask.
answers.sub: New decrees in his hand; the friends you make pay well.

reasons.cpt: Caesar's friends receive what he would have given.
reasons.gal: A decree in Caesar's hand can return Armenia.
reasons.egy: Caesar's hand still writes, and it favours his friends.
reasons.sen: Laws no one saw, issued by one man's pen.
reasons.lbr: The dead tyrant rules through his consul's forgeries.
reasons.eqt: Tax exemptions bought at your door cut the companies' revenues.

situations.title: Dolabella Takes the Fasces
situations.question: Consul, will you accept Dolabella as your colleague, or veto him again?
situations.body: Dolabella has put on the purple border and taken Caesar's fasces. Caesar named him consul for the months of the Parthian war. As augur, you declared the omens against his election. The people cheer him. The consulars count on you to keep the bar.

answers.text: Accept him; the people elected him to the post.
answers.sub: Dolabella sits beside you; the tribes' choice stands.

reasons.plb: The man who stood for debt relief takes the fasces.
reasons.cpt: Caesar named him; Caesar's choice is honoured.
reasons.lbr: Dolabella spoke kindly of the Ides; a friend in office.
reasons.sen: An augur's verdict thrown aside is the mos maiorum broken.
reasons.eqt: The tribune who tried to cancel debts in 47 is consul.
reasons.oct: Another Caesarian claims a share of the inheritance.

answers.gripWhy: The people's vote stands over the augur's objection.

answers.text: Renew your augural veto: the omens forbid him.
answers.sub: Dolabella is no consul; you rule without a colleague.

reasons.sen: The augurs' law stands above a dead man's wish.
reasons.eqt: No debt-canceller holds the fasces.
reasons.plb: The consul blocks the people's man with a bird omen.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's appointment is refused by his own lieutenant.
reasons.lbr: A lone consul ruling by omens looks like a tyrant.

answers.gripWhy: One consul alone, ruling by the augur's word.

situations.title: The Queen's Son
situations.question: Consul, will you name Caesarion Caesar's son before the Senate?
situations.body: Queen Cleopatra keeps Caesar's villa across the Tiber with her son Ptolemy Caesar, three years old. The will does not name him. Crowds jeer her litter. She asks you to declare him Caesar's son in the Curia and to send a Roman escort with her ships.

answers.text: Name him Caesar's son; give her a cohort.
answers.sub: Egypt bound to you; the Senate hears a king's son named.

reasons.egy: Caesarion named Caesar's son: the queen's throne is secured.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's blood honoured, Egypt's gold on their side.
reasons.oct: A second son of Caesar threatens his name and inheritance.
reasons.sen: A foreign queen's child named in the Curia, a king's claim.
reasons.lbr: A royal heir to the tyrant, proclaimed in the Senate.
reasons.plb: The crowd hates the Egyptian queen and her son.

answers.text: No son of Caesar named; let her sail.
answers.sub: No escort, no decree; Rome owes no dynasty to anyone.

reasons.lbr: No dynasty of Caesar, Roman or Egyptian.
reasons.sen: No foreign king's claim enters the Senate's acts.
reasons.oct: Only one son of Caesar is named: himself.
reasons.egy: Her son disowned, her voyage unguarded through Pompeian seas.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's queen and son cast off like strangers.
reasons.par: Egypt left alone weakens the Caesarians in the East.

situations.title: The False Marius
situations.question: Consul, what will you do with the man who calls himself Marius's grandson?
situations.body: A horse-doctor named Herophilus calls himself Amatius, grandson of Gaius Marius. He has raised an altar where Caesar burned. Each night his crowds carry torches to the conspirators' houses. The Senate wants him gone. The Subura calls him Caesar's kinsman.

answers.text: Seize him and put him to death without trial.
answers.sub: His altar torn down; the Senate thanks you in a decree.

reasons.sen: The agitator dies and the altar falls; order returns.
reasons.lbr: Their houses are safe from the torch at last.
reasons.eqt: Riot ends; property is protected by a hard hand.
reasons.plb: A man of the people killed with no trial or appeal.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's cult is struck down by a Caesarian.
reasons.oct: His father's altar is torn down by the consul.

answers.gripWhy: A citizen executed on a consul's order, with no trial.

answers.text: Try him before a praetor's court like any citizen.
answers.sub: Charges of arson and riot; the crowd waits on the verdict.

reasons.lbr: Even a rioter has the law; so do they.
reasons.sen: Courts, not crowds, decide; the Senate approves the form.
reasons.eqt: A trial ends the riots without new bloodshed.
reasons.plb: Their champion stands in the dock while murderers walk free.
reasons.cpt: Treating Caesar's mourners as criminals insults his memory.

answers.gripWhy: The law, not the consul's sword, decides a citizen's life.

answers.text: Leave his altar standing; it is the people's grief.
answers.sub: The cult grows; the conspirators' houses stay under siege.

reasons.plb: Caesar's altar stands, and their kinsman of Marius with it.
reasons.oct: His father becomes a god of the streets.
reasons.cpt: The cult keeps Caesar's cause alive in Rome.
reasons.lbr: Each night the torches come closer to their doors.
reasons.sen: A false Marius rules the Forum while the consul watches.
reasons.eqt: Arson in the city frightens every lender.

situations.title: End the Dictatorship
situations.question: Consul, will you carry the law ending the dictatorship forever?
situations.body: Cicero and the consulars ask for a law that no man may propose or accept the dictatorship. Caesar held it for life. Some of his officers want it next. The Forum still smells of the pyre.

answers.text: Carry the law with the Senate's consent
answers.sub: The office dies; the Senate shares the credit with you.

reasons.sen: The boni see a consul who fears kings as they do.
reasons.eqt: No dictator means no new proscription lists.
reasons.cpt: Lepidus loses an office he hoped to hold.
reasons.oct: Caesar's own title buried by the man holding his papers.
reasons.par: A Rome without a dictator plans no Parthian war.

answers.gripWhy: No man may hold supreme power again.

answers.text: Abolish it and curse whoever seeks a crown
answers.sub: A sacred law: any would-be king may be killed unpunished.

reasons.lbr: The law calls what they did on the Ides lawful.
reasons.sen: Cicero likes the curse, though not who it honours.
reasons.cpt: It names Caesar a tyrant in all but words.
reasons.oct: His father's murderers are blessed by statute.
reasons.plb: The crowd hears Brutus praised over Caesar's ashes.

answers.gripWhy: Any citizen may now strike down a would-be king.

answers.text: Refuse; Rome may need a dictator again
answers.sub: The office stays open for a victorious Caesarian.

reasons.cpt: Lepidus keeps the road to supreme command open.
reasons.oct: His father's office is not erased.
reasons.sen: A consul who keeps the dictatorship is the next tyrant.
reasons.lbr: Proof they killed one tyrant to get another.
reasons.eqt: Bankers smell confiscations under a future dictator.

answers.gripWhy: You keep the door open to rule by one man.

situations.title: Swords at Casilinum

carrier.name: Titus Rufrenus
carrier.role: Veteran centurion of the Seventh, colonists' spokesman

situations.question: Consul, will you survey the veterans' land before Casilinum burns?
situations.body: Caesar promised land to the Seventh and Eighth. At Casilinum and Calatia the old colonists still hold it. Veterans with swords gather at the boundary stones. No surveyor has come since the Ides.

answers.text: Tour the colonies yourself and survey now
answers.sub: You ride south with surveyors; Rome waits a month.

reasons.plb: Land for the poor, staked out by the consul himself.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's soldiers settled by Caesar's consul.
reasons.sen: The consul leaves the city to court armed men.
reasons.eqt: Old colonists' titles, pledged for loans, are cut.
reasons.oct: The veterans thank you, not Caesar's son.

answers.text: Promise them land elsewhere under Caesar's acts
answers.sub: New allotments from Caesar's papers; old colonists keep theirs.

reasons.cpt: Caesar's acts honoured to the letter for his men.
reasons.oct: The veterans learn to wait on your seal, not his.
reasons.eqt: Old titles stand; the debts on them stay good.
reasons.sen: More grants from papers no senator has read.
reasons.plb: Land for soldiers means none for the city poor.

answers.text: Pay them off in silver and send them home
answers.sub: A cash bounty from the Ops treasury; no land seized.

reasons.eqt: Property stands untouched and silver flows to the shops.
reasons.sen: Order kept without new colonies or tribunes' laws.
reasons.cpt: Silver is not the land Caesar swore to them.
reasons.oct: Men who wanted land will remember his offers.
reasons.plb: Coin for soldiers, nothing for the Subura.

situations.title: The Heir at Your Gate
situations.question: Will you hand over Caesar's money and back his adoption law?
situations.body: The boy is eighteen and calls himself Caesar. He waits in the gardens of Pompey's old house, where you live. He wants the money you took from Calpurnia to pay 300 sesterces to every citizen. He wants a curiate law confirming his adoption.

answers.text: Pay him Caesar's money and pass his adoption
answers.sub: Caesar's heir is funded and confirmed by your hand.

reasons.oct: His name, his father, his silver: all granted.
reasons.plb: The bequest will be paid in the Forum.
reasons.egy: A rival heir is crowned; Caesarion fades.
reasons.cpt: A boy now carries Caesar's name over his officers.
reasons.lbr: Caesar's son, paid and confirmed, swears vengeance.

answers.text: Refuse: Caesar's money belongs to the treasury
answers.sub: The chest pays state debts; his adoption waits on law.

reasons.sen: Public money stays public, out of a boy's hands.
reasons.eqt: The treasury pays its creditors first.
reasons.oct: His father's money kept by the man who failed him.
reasons.plb: No 300 sesterces; the crowd blames you.
reasons.lbr: Caesar's heir starved of silver is no avenger.

answers.text: Pay the bequest yourself, in your own name
answers.sub: The people get 300 sesterces from the consul's hand.

reasons.plb: Silver in the Forum, from the consul himself.
reasons.oct: You steal his father's gift and his crowd.
reasons.eqt: The chest empties; the consul's credit looks worse.
reasons.sen: Buying the mob with Caesar's money.
reasons.cpt: The veterans see Caesar's will honoured either way.

situations.title: Armenia for a Bond
situations.question: Will you find this decree in Caesar's papers for ten million sesterces?
situations.body: Deiotarus's envoys brought Fulvia a bond for 10 million sesterces. In return they want a decree, said to be in Caesar's hand, restoring Lesser Armenia to Galatia. Caesar despised the old king. The Senate mutters at acts no one ever saw.

answers.text: Publish the decree from Caesar's papers
answers.sub: The bond is yours; Galatia gets Lesser Armenia.

reasons.gal: The king's lands return; he pays as promised.
reasons.eqt: A paying client king keeps Asian revenues flowing.
reasons.sen: Another forged act, sold over the consul's table.
reasons.lbr: Caesar's tyranny now sold by his executor.
reasons.cpt: Caesar judged Deiotarus; you overrule the dead man.

answers.gripWhy: You rule by a dead man's notebook.

answers.text: Return the bond and let the Senate debate
answers.sub: No secret acts; senators speak freely on the king's claim.

reasons.sen: Caesar's papers answer to free debate, not your house.
reasons.lbr: No man rules Rome from a dead man's notebook.
reasons.gal: No lands, and the king's silver stays home.
reasons.eqt: A rich client loses the hearing he paid for.
reasons.cpt: The Senate sits in judgment on Caesar's acts.

answers.gripWhy: Open debate replaces the consul's private seal.

situations.title: Decimus Holds the North
situations.question: Will you take Cisalpine Gaul from Decimus, and by which road?
situations.body: Decimus Brutus, one of the assassins, holds Cisalpine Gaul with two legions by Caesar's grant. From there an army reaches Rome in days. Six legions wait in Macedonia for a Parthian war that will not come.

answers.text: Ask the Senate to reallot the provinces
answers.sub: A decree for Gaul and the legions, if the consulars agree.

reasons.sen: The Senate allots provinces, as the ancestors did.
reasons.eqt: Lawful change by decree keeps the markets calm.
reasons.lbr: The Senate leans on Decimus to give up his post.
reasons.cpt: Waiting on Cicero's vote while assassins hold armies.
reasons.par: A consul with Macedonian legions can still march east.

answers.text: Take Gaul through the tribal assembly
answers.sub: The tribes vote you Gaul and the legions over the Senate.

reasons.plb: The tribes decide, not the consulars.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's consul takes the army back from an assassin.
reasons.sen: Provinces seized by vote over the Senate's head.
reasons.lbr: Decimus will be ordered out by the crowd's law.
reasons.eqt: A province taken by vote means war loans.

answers.gripWhy: You pass the Senate by with a packed assembly.

answers.text: Leave Decimus in his lawful province
answers.sub: Caesar's grant stands; the amnesty is kept to the letter.

reasons.lbr: Their man keeps his legions and his safety.
reasons.sen: Lawful grants respected; no armed consul in the north.
reasons.cpt: An assassin left with an army on Italy's border.
reasons.oct: The murderers keep Caesar's gift of Gaul.
reasons.par: Romans holding legions against each other suit Orodes.

answers.gripWhy: You hold back from force against a governor.

situations.title: Grain Clerks or Governors
situations.question: Will you send Brutus and Cassius to buy grain abroad?
situations.body: Brutus and Cassius wait at Lanuvium. They are still praetors but cannot safely enter Rome. The consulars propose a commission to buy grain in Asia and Sicily. It would take them out of Italy. Their friends call it a task for freedmen.

answers.text: Give them the grain commission, with honour
answers.sub: A senatorial charge sends them abroad; Italy calms.

reasons.sen: The consulars' compromise passes; the city stays quiet.
reasons.eqt: Grain bought in Asia keeps the price down.
reasons.lbr: A clerk's errand for the men who freed Rome.
reasons.plb: Grain coming, and the assassins gone.
reasons.cpt: They leave alive and unpunished.
reasons.gal: Roman grain buyers in Asia pay well for harvests.

answers.text: Order them out with no office at all
answers.sub: No commission, no province; their praetorships run out empty.

reasons.cpt: Caesar's killers stripped bare.
reasons.oct: No reward for his father's murderers.
reasons.plb: The crowd cheers them hounded from Italy.
reasons.lbr: Driven out with nothing, they must take armies themselves.
reasons.sen: The amnesty broken in all but name.
reasons.par: Desperate Liberators in the East mean Roman war.

answers.gripWhy: You break the amnesty's spirit by force of office.

answers.text: Give them real provinces: Crete and Cyrene
answers.sub: Governors with rank, far away, and honoured for it.

reasons.lbr: Provinces, rank and safety: the amnesty means something.
reasons.sen: Honour kept for men of the first families.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's murderers rewarded with governorships.
reasons.plb: The killers sent off in purple as governors.
reasons.egy: Liberators in Cyrene sit on Egypt's border.
reasons.par: Friends of Parthia gain seats nearer Syria.

situations.title: The Board of Seven

carrier.name: Lucius Antonius
carrier.role: Head of the board of seven for land distribution

situations.question: Brother, which land will you give the veterans and the poor?
situations.body: Your agrarian law gives the board of seven land for veterans and the poor. The public land of Campania pays rents to the treasury. The Pontine marshes are not yet drained. Estates of Pompeians and absent conspirators lie empty.

answers.text: Divide the Campanian public land now
answers.sub: Allotments this summer; the treasury loses Campania's rents.

reasons.plb: Land this summer, near Rome, for the poor.
reasons.cpt: Veterans share the best soil in Italy.
reasons.eqt: The rent contracts of Campania are torn up.
reasons.sen: The last great public estate handed to the crowd.
reasons.oct: Land given in the Antonian name, not Caesar's.

answers.text: Take the estates of Pompeians and absent assassins
answers.sub: Confiscation, as Caesar's victory allowed; colonists move in now.

reasons.cpt: The defeated pay the victors, as in Caesar's day.
reasons.oct: His father's killers lose their lands.
reasons.plb: More land for the poor, taken from the rich.
reasons.lbr: Their estates seized; the amnesty is dead.
reasons.eqt: Private fortunes seized: the thing they fear most.
reasons.sen: Property is no longer safe in Italy.

answers.gripWhy: Seizing estates puts soldiers at the gates.

answers.text: Drain the Pontine marshes first
answers.sub: No one's land is taken; allotments wait two years.

reasons.eqt: Drainage contracts for the companies, no estate touched.
reasons.sen: Public works, not confiscations, settle the soldiers.
reasons.plb: Two years of waiting for marsh mud.
reasons.cpt: Veterans promised land now get ditches.
reasons.oct: Restless veterans will hear his offers sooner.

situations.title: Centurions on the Benches

carrier.name: Publius Aufidius
carrier.role: Spokesman of the Asian tax companies

situations.question: Will you put centurions of the Alaudae on the jury panels?
situations.body: Your bill adds a third panel of jurors: centurions and soldiers of the Alaudae, the legion raised from Gauls. Senators and equites now share the courts. The companies of Asia say no contract or debt case will be safe.

answers.text: Pass it: Caesar's soldiers sit in judgment
answers.sub: Alaudae men judge cases; the courts lean your way.

reasons.cpt: Caesar's men judge, not the men who hated him.
reasons.plb: Common men on the benches at last.
reasons.eqt: Their hold on the courts broken by soldiers.
reasons.sen: Gallic legionaries sitting in judgment on senators.
reasons.lbr: Any charge against them now meets Caesar's soldiers.

answers.gripWhy: Soldiers in the courts make the law yours.

answers.text: Withdraw the bill; senators and equites judge
answers.sub: The courts stay with the propertied orders.

reasons.eqt: Their courts and contracts stay safe.
reasons.sen: Judgment stays with the orders that own Rome.
reasons.cpt: The veterans shut out of the courts again.
reasons.plb: The benches stay with the rich.

situations.title: Accius at the Games
situations.question: Will you let the theatre open with Accius's play on the kings?
situations.body: The Ludi Apollinares belong to Brutus as urban praetor, but he dares not enter Rome. Your brother Gaius presides in his place. Brutus asks that the games open with Accius's play on the driving out of the kings.

answers.text: Let the play run as Brutus asks
answers.sub: The crowd hears liberty; Brutus's name is cheered.

reasons.lbr: Their games, their play, their cause cheered in Rome.
reasons.sen: A praetor's games run as custom demands.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's killers applauded under your eyes.
reasons.oct: The theatre cheers his father's murderers.
reasons.plb: The Subura came for mimes, not lectures on kings.

answers.gripWhy: Free speech on the stage, unpoliced.

answers.text: Stage another play, with mimes and free seats
answers.sub: Bread and shows; Brutus's lines are never heard.

reasons.plb: Free shows and food at the games.
reasons.cpt: No praise of assassins on a Roman stage.
reasons.lbr: Even their own games are taken from them.
reasons.sen: A praetor's rights overridden by the consul.

answers.gripWhy: You censor the praetor's own games.

situations.title: The Golden Chair

carrier.name: Lucius Varenus
carrier.role: Attendant (viator) of a tribune of the plebs

situations.question: The heir wants Caesar's chair in the theatre. Will you allow it?
situations.body: Ludi Victoriae Caesaris, July. Octavian orders Caesar's golden chair and jewelled wreath set among the seats, as the Senate once decreed. Two tribunes threaten their veto. Above the city a comet burns for the seventh night. The crowd calls it Caesar's soul among the gods.

answers.text: Set the chair; Caesar sits among the gods.
answers.sub: The star is Caesar's; the heir shares your glory.

reasons.oct: My father's chair seen by all Rome: my name grows.
reasons.plb: The star is Caesar's soul; the crowd cheers his chair.
reasons.cpt: Caesar honoured, his acts safe; the veterans see it.
reasons.lbr: A god's throne for the tyrant we struck down.
reasons.sen: Honours of a king again, in a free theatre.

answers.text: Forbid it: Rome honours no kings, living or dead.
answers.sub: No divine honours; the dictator's regalia stay locked away.

reasons.lbr: No god's honours for the tyrant: our deed stands.
reasons.sen: A consul refusing regal show steadies the Republic.
reasons.oct: You insult my father before the people; I won't forget.
reasons.plb: Caesar's star burns and you hide his chair?
reasons.cpt: Caesar's men see his honours refused by his own consul.

answers.text: Let the tribunes' veto stand, by law.
answers.sub: The college of tribunes decides; you keep clear of it.

reasons.sen: The veto respected, custom kept: the Senate approves.
reasons.eqt: No quarrel at the games; markets stay calm.
reasons.lbr: Caesar denied his chair, and by lawful means.
reasons.oct: You hide behind tribunes to deny my father.
reasons.plb: Tribunes blocking Caesar's chair? Not our tribunes.

answers.gripWhy: You leave the decision to the tribunes' veto.

situations.title: Bread at the Wharves
situations.question: The price of grain has doubled. How will you feed Rome?
situations.body: The Sicilian and Alexandrian ships are three weeks late. At the Tiber wharves a modius sells at twice the spring price. The 150,000 names on the free list are full by Caesar's law. Crowds gather at the Porticus Minucia. Granaries on the Aventine are said to be locked.

answers.text: Raise the list above 150,000 by a tribune's law.
answers.sub: Lucius Antonius carries it; the poor of the Subura eat.

reasons.plb: More names on the list: bread for the Subura.
reasons.cpt: Fed plebs keep the city quiet for Caesar's party.
reasons.eqt: A bigger dole means new taxes on us.
reasons.sen: A tribune's law over our heads, buying the mob.
reasons.oct: The consul feeds the people while my bequest waits.

answers.text: Let the aediles buy grain by Senate decree.
answers.sub: Treasury silver buys at market; the list stays as Caesar fixed.

reasons.sen: Grain by decree, through the aediles, as custom requires.
reasons.eqt: The shippers sell at market price, paid in silver.
reasons.plb: Bread for the listed; the rest of us starve.
reasons.cpt: The Senate takes the credit for feeding Rome.

answers.text: Order the queen's grain and seize the hoarders' stores.
answers.sub: Alexandria ships at once; locked granaries are opened by soldiers.

reasons.plb: The hoarders punished and bread on the wharves.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's way: soldiers, grain and a grateful city.
reasons.egy: Egypt's grain is a gift, not a Roman's command.
reasons.eqt: Soldiers opening private granaries: property is no longer safe.
reasons.sen: Soldiers in the warehouses, by the consul's word alone.

answers.gripWhy: Soldiers break open private granaries on the Aventine.

situations.title: The Commission on the Papers
situations.question: Piso demands a commission on Caesar's papers. Will you submit to it?
situations.body: Kalends of August. Lucius Piso, Caesar's own father-in-law, rose in the Senate and attacked your conduct. Hundreds of acts have been posted from the notebooks since March. The consulars want a commission to examine each one. Under the June law, that power is yours.

answers.text: Grant the commission; the consulars review every act.
answers.sub: The Senate sits in judgment on what you posted.

reasons.sen: Our authority restored: no act without the Senate's review.
reasons.eqt: Valid contracts sorted from forgeries; credit can breathe.
reasons.lbr: Every forgery exposed weakens the tyrant's acts.
reasons.gal: The decree restoring Armenia may die in committee.
reasons.cpt: Caesar's grants judged by the men who hated him.
